en: Theravāda Vinaya Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga Pācittiyakaṇḍa
Cittāgāra-vagga 41.
The Training Rule on Royal Palaces.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a painted picture had been made in the Painted Hall (*cittāgāra*) in King Pasenadi of Kosala’s park.
Many people were going to see the Painted Hall.
The group of six bhikkhunīs also went to see the Painted Hall.
People complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying,
“How can these bhikkhunīs go to see a pleasure grove, just like householders who indulge in sensual pleasures?
The bhikkhunīs heard those people complaining, grumbling, and spreading it about.
Those bhikkhunīs who were modest … [as above] … complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How can the bhikkhunīs of the group of six go to see a picture gallery? … [The Buddha asked:
“Is it true, bhikkhus, that the bhikkhunīs of the group of six go to see a picture gallery?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can it be, monks, that the group-of-six bhikkhunīs go to see a picture gallery?”
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And thus, monks, should the nuns recite this training rule:
‘If any bhikkhunī should go to see a royal palace, a picture gallery, a park, a garden, or a lotus pond, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).’”
"But whichever" means whichever such...
"nun" means... [as before].
...pe... this is the nun intended in this context.
"Royal palace" means:
wherever it has been built for a king to play or to enjoy himself.
A "hall" (*cittāgāra*) is any place built for people to play and enjoy themselves.
A "grove" (*ārāma*) is...
A pleasure garden (*uyyāna*) is any place made for people to play and enjoy themselves.
A park (*ārāma*) is any place made for people to play and enjoy themselves.
A "lotus pond" is one made anywhere for people to play and enjoy themselves. If one goes there for the purpose of seeing it,
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Wherever she stands and sees [them], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If she goes beyond the range of sight and sees them again and again, there is an offense of expiation.
If she goes to see each one individually, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Wherever she stands and sees [him], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If, having left the range of sight, she sees him again and again, there is an offense of expiation.
There is no offense—
Standing in the monastery, she sees him;
or going or coming, she sees him;
or having gone on some business, she sees him.
In cases of misfortune,
for one who is insane,
and for one who is a first-time offender.
The first training rule is concluded.
